title: Social and Anti-Social Housing | Samuel Stein
gist: Comparing New York's public and union-cooperative housing legacy to Vienna's far larger and cheaper-per-resident social housing system, Samuel Stein argues Vienna spends less per resident specifically because it suppresses land values and buys land before developing non-profit housing, while NYC's subsidy schemes are structured to guarantee profit at every stage — a gap now driving new social-housing-developer legislation in New York, Rhode Island, and Seattle.

themes.theme: The scale and structure of NYC public housing

insights.claim: New York City's public housing authority operates over 150,000 apartments across hundreds of developments, the largest public housing program in the U.S. by both absolute unit count and share of total housing stock; about 13% of the stock has since moved to private management via a local version of the federal Rental Assistance Demonstration program.
insights.speaker: Samuel Stein
insights.so_what: Establishes the scale of a major, still largely public housing stock that has resisted the nationwide trend of demolition/privatization — relevant to any analysis of NYC real estate supply, RAD conversions, or municipal housing finance.
insights.quote: With over 150,000 apartments in hundreds of developments across the five boroughs, the New York City Public Housing Authority's program is the largest in the country.

insights.claim: Nearly 300,000 New Yorkers live in the public housing system (an official, likely undercounted figure) — a population roughly the size of Pittsburgh, larger than the city's homeless population, which is roughly the size of Boulder.
insights.speaker: Samuel Stein
insights.so_what: A striking comparative-scale statistic underscoring how much stability the public housing system provides to NYC's working class relative to the scale of the city's homelessness crisis.
insights.quote: the population living in New York City's public housing is roughly the size of Pittsburgh.

insights.claim: New York's public housing began as a purely municipal (not federal) initiative before the New Deal, starting with the demolition and rebuilding of Lower East Side tenements purchased from the Astor family ('First Houses'); the subsequent federalized New Deal model imposed a one-to-one demolition-to-construction 'urban renewal' rule that displaced residents (disproportionately Black and immigrant) even as it built a working-class housing base that reached as much as a third of the rental stock in neighborhoods like East Harlem.
insights.speaker: Samuel Stein
insights.so_what: Explains a structural design flaw (forced demolition ratio) baked into the federal public housing model from its origin, useful context for understanding why urban renewal-era displacement occurred alongside housing construction.
insights.quote: This created a flood of internally displaced residents at a pace that constantly overwhelmed the city's resettlement authority.
insights.locator: paragraph on the New Deal urban renewal model

insights.claim: The author argues that chronic federal underfunding, not any inherent flaw of public ownership, caused deferred maintenance and dangerous conditions in public housing, contrary to mainstream framing that treats such failures as an inevitable outcome of government-run housing.
insights.speaker: Samuel Stein
insights.so_what: A direct rebuttal to the common narrative used to justify privatizing public housing, relevant to assessing the policy case for and against further RAD-style conversions.
insights.quote: Rather than understand this as the consequence of stingy and regressive budgeting, however, mainstream politicians and pundits have cast it as the inevitable outcome of public ownership.

themes.theme: Union cooperatives and the Mitchell-Lama program

insights.claim: New York's union cooperative movement — led by the garment workers' United Housing Foundation and joined by electrical, butcher, typesetter, furrier, and health-care worker unions — produced roughly 50,000 homes as limited-equity cooperatives, many bundled with an entire 'solidarity economy' of pharmacies, health clinics, daycare, grocery links to allied farms, bakeries, and in one case even an alternative to municipal policing.
insights.speaker: Samuel Stein
insights.so_what: Documents a historical, union-financed alternative housing-plus-services model at meaningful scale (50,000 homes) that could inform current labor-sponsored housing development proposals.
insights.quote: the operator of an industry-financed welfare state that supplies cradle-to-grave protection for the families of 30,000 members.
insights.locator: quoted description of the electricians' cooperative

insights.claim: New York State's Mitchell-Lama program (mid-1950s to early 1980s) produced 69,000 cooperative apartments and 66,000 rental homes using tax breaks, bond financing, and low-interest loans for limited-profit developers.
insights.speaker: Samuel Stein
insights.so_what: Quantifies a specific, replicable state-level subsidized-housing financing model (tax breaks + bonds + low-interest loans) that produced over 135,000 units — a template referenced by current 'Mitchell-Lama 2.0' proposals.
insights.quote: From the mid-1950s to the early 1980s, the program produced 69,000 cooperative apartments and 66,000 rental homes.

insights.claim: Mitchell-Lama's built-in 'sunset clause' allowed owners to exit the affordability program once the mortgage was paid off; more than half of rentals and roughly 10% of co-ops have since left the program, prompting tenant activist John Leyva to rename it a 'doomsday clause.'
insights.speaker: Samuel Stein
insights.so_what: A concrete mechanism showing how a seemingly neutral contract term (a mortgage-payoff exit clause) can structurally erode a subsidized housing stock over decades — a design flaw relevant to any future affordable-housing bond/tax-abatement program.
insights.quote: I don't call it a sunset because sunsets are beautiful. I call it a 'doomsday' clause.

insights.claim: Few co-op residents exited the Mitchell-Lama program even when eligible, suggesting residents valued the use-value of home and community over potential windfall profit, whereas most eligible rental landlords did opt out — implying that for landlords, a building's use-value is simply its exchange-value.
insights.speaker: Samuel Stein
insights.so_what: A clean natural experiment in ownership incentives (resident-owner vs. landlord behavior under identical exit options) relevant to designing future limited-equity housing programs to resist erosion.
insights.quote: for landlords, their building's use value is its exchange value.
insights.locator: paragraph on cooperative vs. rental landlord exit behavior

insights.claim: Vienna's social housing stock is approximately 43% of the city's total housing, versus roughly 9% in New York City; Vienna's inclusionary zoning requires two-thirds of new development to be social housing, compared to NYC's one-third requirement, and social housing is eligible to all residents after just two years of stable residency, including in emergency shelters.
insights.speaker: Samuel Stein
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale gap between the two cities' social housing systems, providing a concrete benchmark for what a much larger U.S. social housing sector could look like.
insights.quote: Suddenly our 9 percent social housing stock seemed paltry compared to their 43 percent.

insights.claim: Vienna's new social housing developments require less subsidy per resident than New York's despite Vienna's far larger scale, because Vienna actively suppresses land and property values and buys land before subsidizing non-profit construction, whereas New York's subsidy schemes are structured to guarantee profits for landowners, landlords, and other stakeholders at every stage.
insights.speaker: Samuel Stein
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, replicable policy mechanism (pre-emptive land banking + non-profit-only development) that lowers per-resident subsidy cost — directly actionable for any U.S. jurisdiction designing a new social housing authority.
insights.quote: Vienna takes active measures to cool land and property values, then buys land and subsidizes construction for housing that is never meant to turn a profit—whereas we construct subsidy schemes meant to ensure profits for an array of stakeholders, from landowner to landlord.
insights.locator: paragraph on why Vienna needs less subsidy

insights.claim: Uruguay's Federation of Housing Cooperatives for Mutual Aid, active since 1970, is cited as another strong (if less internationally heralded) model of self-built cooperative social housing.
insights.speaker: Samuel Stein
insights.so_what: Flags an additional, lesser-known international social-housing model worth benchmarking beyond the more commonly cited Vienna case.

themes.theme: A new U.S. social housing movement

insights.claim: New York tenant and homeless advocacy groups have drafted a bill to create a Social Housing Development Authority for New York State, modeled on the Labor Housing Conference, that could build new social housing and acquire/convert existing buildings; as of writing it remains far from passing but represents the first collectively asserted positive vision for new housing construction from the NY housing left in a generation.
insights.speaker: Samuel Stein
insights.so_what: A specific piece of pending state legislation to track as a potential catalyst for a large new social-housing development vehicle in New York.
insights.quote: it is the first time in a generation (if not longer) that the New York housing left has collectively asserted a positive vision for new housing construction.
insights.locator: paragraph on the proposed Social Housing Development Authority

insights.claim: Similar social-housing-developer initiatives are underway elsewhere in the U.S.: Reclaim RI is pushing to convert Rhode Island's Department of Housing into a public developer with power to build mixed-income public housing, and Seattle voters approved creating and funding a new municipal social housing developer.
insights.speaker: Samuel Stein
insights.so_what: Signals a broader, multi-city/state U.S. trend toward reviving public/social housing development as of 2026 — relevant to municipal-bond and public housing policy investors tracking this emerging asset class.
insights.quote: residents voted to create and fund a new municipal social housing developer.
insights.locator: paragraph on Rhode Island and Seattle initiatives

insights.claim: Citing sociologist Ralph Miliband, the author argues the capitalist state will not voluntarily deliver a right to housing because it is 'constructed specifically to avoid this outcome,' and that only organized working-class pressure can force the state to change.
insights.speaker: Samuel Stein
insights.so_what: Frames the political-economy thesis underlying the piece: expect social housing expansion to come only through sustained organized pressure, not voluntary state action, relevant to timelines for any such policy materializing.
insights.quote: If this state will not deliver a right to housing, we must do the work to bring about a state that will.
